Tuple Relational Calculus

Chapters 8 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 8.24–8.30. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

Relational algebra says how to compute an answer; relational calculus says what the answer is: the set of tuples that satisfy a condition. The two are equally expressive, so any query can be written in either. “For all” is the hard part. Write it as “there is no counterexample”, and guard every universally quantified variable with an implication.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  Relational calculus at a glance

    Theory recap
    Definition: Relational calculus

    A declarative (nonprocedural) formal query language based on first-order predicate logic. One expression states what is to be retrieved, not how or in what order. Relational algebra (RA), by contrast, is procedural: an expression fixes an order of operations.

    • Tuple relational calculus (TRC), Section 8.6: variables range over tuples of relations. SQL is based on TRC.
    • Domain relational calculus (DRC), Section 8.7: variables range over single attribute values. QBE is based on DRC.
    How RA and calculus relate (Exercise 8.8)

    Same expressive power: any query of the basic RA can be written in TRC/DRC, and any safe calculus expression can be written in basic RA. Different style: RA builds the answer by a sequence of operations (procedural); calculus describes the property the answer tuples must satisfy (declarative). A language is relationally complete if it can express every query expressible in relational calculus (equivalently basic RA). SQL is relationally complete and has more (aggregates, grouping, ordering), which neither basic RA nor calculus has. Calculus matters because it rests on mathematical logic and because SQL rests on it.

    2  Tuple relational calculus: syntax and meaning

    Theory recap

    Tuple variables and range relations (8.6.1)

    Definition: Tuple variable, range relation, simple TRC query

    A tuple variable takes as its value an individual tuple. Its range relation RRR is stated by the condition R(t)R(t)R(t), read “ttt is a tuple of RRR”. The simplest query is

    { t∣COND(t) }\{\,t \mid \mathrm{COND}(t)\,\}{t∣COND(t)}

    whose result is the set of all tuples ttt for which the Boolean formula COND(t)\mathrm{COND}(t)COND(t) is TRUE.

    Salary above 50000, all attributes / some attributes
    { t∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000 }{ t.Fname, t.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000 }\begin{gathered}\{\,t \mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\textsf{Salary} > 50000\,\}\\ \{\,t.\textsf{Fname},\ t.\textsf{Lname} \mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\textsf{Salary} > 50000\,\}\end{gathered}{t∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000}{t.Fname, t.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000}​

    t.Salaryt.\textsf{Salary}t.Salary is the book’s notation for t[Salary]t[\mathit{Salary}]t[Salary], like a qualified column t.Salary in SQL. On Figure 5.6 the result is only James Borg (55000).

    A TRC expression must specify three things:

    1. for each tuple variable ttt, its range relation R(t)R(t)R(t) (without it, ttt ranges over every tuple in the universe);
    2. a condition selecting the wanted combinations of tuples (selection conditions and join conditions);
    3. the requested attributes (the target list, left of the bar).
    Query 0: birth date and address of John B. Smith
    Q0: { t.Bdate, t.Address∣ EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Fname=‘John’andt.Minit=‘B’andt.Lname=‘Smith’ }\begin{aligned}Q0:\ \{\,t.\textsf{Bdate},\ t.\textsf{Address} \mid\ &\mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\textsf{Fname}=\text{`John'}\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\textsf{Minit}=\text{`B'} \mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\textsf{Lname}=\text{`Smith'}\,\}\end{aligned}Q0: {t.Bdate, t.Address∣ ​EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Fname=‘John’andt.Minit=‘B’andt.Lname=‘Smith’}​

    Result: (1965-01-09, 731 Fondren, Houston, TX).
    RA: πBdate, Address(σFname=‘John’ ∧ Minit=‘B’ ∧ Lname=‘Smith’(EMPLOYEE))\pi_{\text{Bdate, Address}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Fname=`John' $\wedge$ Minit=`B' $\wedge$ Lname=`Smith'}}\left(EMPLOYEE\right)\right)πBdate, Address​(σFname=‘John’ ∧ Minit=‘B’ ∧ Lname=‘Smith’​(EMPLOYEE)).

    Expressions, atoms and formulas (8.6.2)

    A general TRC expression has the form

    { t1.Aj, t2.Ak, …, tn.Am∣COND(t1,…,tn,tn+1,…,tn+m) }\{\,t_1.A_j,\ t_2.A_k,\ \dots,\ t_n.A_m \mid \mathrm{COND}(t_1,\dots,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots,t_{n+m})\,\}{t1​.Aj​, t2​.Ak​, …, tn​.Am​∣COND(t1​,…,tn​,tn+1​,…,tn+m​)}

    where each AiA_iAi​ is an attribute of the relation over which tit_iti​ ranges and COND is a formula (well-formed formula, WFF). Variables tn+1,…,tn+mt_{n+1},\dots,t_{n+m}tn+1​,…,tn+m​ appear only in the condition and must be quantified there.

    Definition: Atom (three kinds)
    1. R(ti)R(t_i)R(ti​): TRUE iff tit_iti​ is a tuple of relation RRR (the range atom).
    2. ti.A op tj.Bt_i.A \ \mathit{op}\ t_j.Bti​.A op tj​.B, with op∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,≠}\mathit{op}\in\{=,<,\le,>,\ge,\neq\}op∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,=} (typically a join condition).
    3. ti.A op ct_i.A \ \mathit{op}\ cti​.A op c or c op tj.Bc \ \mathit{op}\ t_j.Bc op tj​.B, with ccc a constant (a selection condition).

    Each atom has a truth value (TRUE/FALSE) for a given assignment of tuples to the variables.

    Definition: Formula (Rules 1–4)

    Rule 1: every atom is a formula. Rule 2: if F1F_1F1​, F2F_2F2​ are formulas, so are (F1andF2)(F_1 \mathbin{\textbf{and}} F_2)(F1​andF2​), (F1orF2)(F_1 \mathbin{\textbf{or}} F_2)(F1​orF2​), not (F1)\textbf{not}\, (F_1)not(F1​), not (F2)\textbf{not}\, (F_2)not(F2​), with the usual truth tables. Rule 3: if FFF is a formula, so is (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F); it is TRUE if FFF is TRUE for at least one tuple assigned to the free occurrences of ttt in FFF. Rule 4: if FFF is a formula, so is (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F); it is TRUE if FFF is TRUE for every tuple in the universe assigned to the free occurrences of ttt in FFF.

    Free and bound variables (8.6.3)

    Definition: Free / bound

    An occurrence of ttt in an atom is free. In (F1andF2)(F_1\mathbin{\textbf{and}} F_2)(F1​andF2​), (F1orF2)(F_1\mathbin{\textbf{or}} F_2)(F1​orF2​), not F1\textbf{not}\, F_1notF1​ an occurrence keeps the status it has in F1F_1F1​ or F2F_2F2​ (so a variable can be free in F1F_1F1​ and bound in F2F_2F2​). All free occurrences of ttt in FFF become bound in (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F) or (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F).

    The book’s three formulas

    F1: d.Dname=‘Research’F_1:\ d.\textsf{Dname}=\text{`Research'}F1​: d.Dname=‘Research’    F2: (∃t)(d.Dnumber=t.Dno)F_2:\ (\exists t)(d.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno})F2​: (∃t)(d.Dnumber=t.Dno)    F3: (∀d)(d.Mgr_ssn=‘333445555’)F_3:\ (\forall d)(d.\textsf{Mgr\_ssn}=\text{`333445555'})F3​: (∀d)(d.Mgr_ssn=‘333445555’)
    ddd is free in F1F_1F1​ and F2F_2F2​ and bound (to ∀\forall∀) in F3F_3F3​; ttt is bound (to ∃\exists∃) in F2F_2F2​.

    The golden rule

    The only free variables of a TRC expression must be those that appear left of the bar. Every other variable must be bound by ∃\exists∃ or ∀\forall∀. Free variables play the role of the SQL FROM clause of the outer query; ∃\exists∃-bound variables are like a correlated EXISTS subquery.

    The quantifiers and the transformation rules (8.6.3, 8.6.6)

    Existential (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F)Universal (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F)
    Reads“there exists (at least one) ttt such that FFF”“for every ttt (in the universe), FFF”
    TRUE whenFFF is TRUE for some assignment of tttFFF is TRUE for every assignment of ttt
    Empty rangeFALSE (nothing exists)TRUE (“vacuously”)
    Evaluationany(F(t) for t in U)all(F(t) for t in U)
    Typical bodyR(t)andR(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}R(t)and conditionsnot R(t)ornot (filter)or\textbf{not}\, R(t) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \textbf{not}\, (\text{filter}) \mathbin{\textbf{or}}notR(t)ornot(filter)or condition
    SQL analogueEXISTS (…)NOT EXISTS (… NOT EXISTS …)

    General transformation (informal): swap one quantifier for the other by putting not \textbf{not}\,not in front; and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and and or\mathbin{\textbf{or}}or replace each other; a negated formula becomes un-negated and vice versa. Special cases (≡\equiv≡ means “equivalent to”):

    (∀x)(P(x))  ≡  not (∃x)(not P(x))(∃x)(P(x))  ≡  not (∀x)(not P(x))(∀x)(P(x)andQ(x))  ≡  not (∃x)(not P(x)ornot Q(x))(∀x)(P(x)orQ(x))  ≡  not (∃x)(not P(x)andnot Q(x))(∃x)(P(x)orQ(x))  ≡  not (∀x)(not P(x)andnot Q(x))(∃x)(P(x)andQ(x))  ≡  not (∀x)(not P(x)ornot Q(x))(if P then Q)  ≡  (not PorQ)(implication, written P⇒Q)not (P⇒Q)  ≡  (Pandnot Q)\begin{array}{rcl} (\forall x)(P(x)) &\;\equiv\;& \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x))\\ (\exists x)(P(x)) &\;\equiv\;& \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x))\\ (\forall x)(P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q(x)) &\;\equiv\;& \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \textbf{not}\, Q(x))\\ (\forall x)(P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q(x)) &\;\equiv\;& \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \textbf{not}\, Q(x))\\ (\exists x)(P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q(x)) &\;\equiv\;& \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \textbf{not}\, Q(x))\\ (\exists x)(P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q(x)) &\;\equiv\;& \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \textbf{not}\, Q(x))\\ (\textbf{if } P \textbf{ then } Q) &\;\equiv\;& (\textbf{not}\, P \mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q)\qquad\text{(implication, written } P\Rightarrow Q)\\ \textbf{not}\, (P \Rightarrow Q) &\;\equiv\;& (P \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \textbf{not}\, Q) \end{array}(∀x)(P(x))(∃x)(P(x))(∀x)(P(x)andQ(x))(∀x)(P(x)orQ(x))(∃x)(P(x)orQ(x))(∃x)(P(x)andQ(x))(if P then Q)not(P⇒Q)​≡≡≡≡≡≡≡≡​not(∃x)(notP(x))not(∀x)(notP(x))not(∃x)(notP(x)ornotQ(x))not(∃x)(notP(x)andnotQ(x))not(∀x)(notP(x)andnotQ(x))not(∀x)(notP(x)ornotQ(x))(notPorQ)(implication, written P⇒Q)(PandnotQ)​

    Also TRUE (one direction only; ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ = implies): (∀x)(P(x))⇒(∃x)(P(x))(\forall x)(P(x)) \Rightarrow (\exists x)(P(x))(∀x)(P(x))⇒(∃x)(P(x)) and not (∃x)(P(x))⇒not (∀x)(P(x))\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(P(x)) \Rightarrow \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(P(x))not(∃x)(P(x))⇒not(∀x)(P(x)). (Strictly these need a non-empty universe; the universe of all tuples is never empty.)

    The one derivation to know by heart

    “For every xxx in RRR satisfying CCC, QQQ holds”:

    (∀x)(not R(x)ornot C(x)orQ(x))  ≡  not (∃x)(R(x)andC(x)andnot Q(x))(\forall x)\big(\textbf{not}\, R(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \textbf{not}\, C(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q(x)\big) \;\equiv\; \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)\big(R(x) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} C(x) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \textbf{not}\, Q(x)\big)(∀x)(notR(x)ornotC(x)orQ(x))≡not(∃x)(R(x)andC(x)andnotQ(x))

    Step: ∀=not ∃not \forall = \textbf{not}\, \exists \textbf{not}\,∀=not∃not; then De Morgan turns not (not Rornot CorQ)\textbf{not}\, (\textbf{not}\, R \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \textbf{not}\, C \mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q)not(notRornotCorQ) into (RandCandnot Q)(R \mathbin{\textbf{and}} C \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \textbf{not}\, Q)(RandCandnotQ). In words: “there is no xxx in RRR with CCC that fails QQQ”. Write this line in the exam; graders reward it.

    3  The textbook’s TRC queries · 8.6.4, 8.6.7

    Theory recap

    Each query is given with an English reading, the RA equivalent and its result on Figure 5.6. All results were checked by a Python evaluator that lets every variable range over the whole database (with extra “phantom” tuples that belong to no relation, to imitate the universe) and evaluates ∃\exists∃/∀\forall∀ as any/all.

    Existential queries

    Query 1: name and address of employees of the Research department
    Q1: { t.Fname,t.Lname,t.Address∣ EMPLOYEE(t)and(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)andd.Dname=‘Research’andd.Dnumber=t.Dno) }\begin{aligned}Q1:\ \{\,t.\textsf{Fname},t.\textsf{Lname},t.\textsf{Address}\mid\ &\mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} (\exists d)\big(\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(d)\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}} d.\textsf{Dname}=\text{`Research'} \mathbin{\textbf{and}} d.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno}\big)\,\}\end{aligned}Q1: {t.Fname,t.Lname,t.Address∣ ​EMPLOYEE(t)and(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)andd.Dname=‘Research’andd.Dnumber=t.Dno)}​

    Reading: employees ttt for which there is a department ddd named Research whose number is ttt’s department. ttt is the only free variable. d.Dname=‘Research’d.\textsf{Dname}=\text{`Research'}d.Dname=‘Research’ is a selection condition, d.Dnumber=t.Dnod.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno}d.Dnumber=t.Dno a join condition.
    RA: πFname, Lname, Address(σDname=‘Research’(DEPARTMENT)⋈Dnumber=DnoEMPLOYEE)\pi_{\text{Fname, Lname, Address}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Dname=`Research'}}\left(DEPARTMENT\right) \mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Dnumber=Dno}}} EMPLOYEE\right)πFname, Lname, Address​(σDname=‘Research’​(DEPARTMENT)⋈Dnumber=Dno​EMPLOYEE).
    Result: John Smith, Franklin Wong, Ramesh Narayan, Joyce English (with their addresses).

    Q2: { p.Pnumber,p.Dnum,m.Lname,m.Bdate,m.Address∣PROJECT(p)andEMPLOYEE(m)andp.Plocation=‘Stafford’and(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)andp.Dnum=d.Dnumberandd.Mgr_ssn=m.Ssn) }\begin{aligned}Q2:\ \{\, & p.\textsf{Pnumber},p.\textsf{Dnum},m.\textsf{Lname},m.\textsf{Bdate},m.\textsf{Address} \mid{}\\ &\quad \mathrm{PROJECT}(p) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(m) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} p.\textsf{Plocation}=\text{`Stafford'}\\ &\quad \mathbin{\textbf{and}} (\exists d)\big(\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(d) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} p.\textsf{Dnum}=d.\textsf{Dnumber} \mathbin{\textbf{and}} d.\textsf{Mgr\_ssn}=m.\textsf{Ssn}\big)\,\}\end{aligned}Q2: {​p.Pnumber,p.Dnum,m.Lname,m.Bdate,m.Address∣PROJECT(p)andEMPLOYEE(m)andp.Plocation=‘Stafford’and(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)andp.Dnum=d.Dnumberandd.Mgr_ssn=m.Ssn)}​

    Universal quantification: Query 3 (8.6.7)

    Query 3: employees who work on all projects controlled by department 5
    Q3: { e.Lname,e.Fname∣ EMPLOYEE(e)and(∀x)(not PROJECT(x)ornot (x.Dnum=5)or(∃w)(WORKS_ON(w)andw.Essn=e.Ssnandx.Pnumber=w.Pno)) }\begin{aligned}Q3:\ \{\,e.\textsf{Lname},e.\textsf{Fname} \mid\ & \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(e) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} (\forall x)\Big(\textbf{not}\, \mathrm{PROJECT}(x) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \textbf{not}\, (x.\textsf{Dnum}=5)\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{or}} (\exists w)\big(\mathrm{WORKS\_ON}(w)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}w.\textsf{Essn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}\\ &\qquad \mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Pnumber}=w.\textsf{Pno}\big)\Big)\,\}\end{aligned}Q3: {e.Lname,e.Fname∣ ​EMPLOYEE(e)and(∀x)(notPROJECT(x)ornot(x.Dnum=5)or(∃w)(WORKS_ON(w)andw.Essn=e.Ssnandx.Pnumber=w.Pno))}​

    with the result’s Essn matched to Ssn.
    Result on Figure 5.6: empty. Department 5 controls projects 1, 2, 3; nobody works on all three (Smith/English: 1, 2; Wong: 2, 3; Narayan: 3). The same formula with department 4 (projects 10, 30) returns Alicia Zelaya and Ahmad Jabbar.

    Vacuous truth: the “for all” edge case

    If no tuple passes the filter (for example a department that controls no projects), the ∀\forall∀ condition is TRUE for every employee, so all employees are returned (checked: department 7 returns all 8 employees). This is the same as RA division by an empty divisor and SQL NOT EXISTS over an empty set. State it as an assumption whenever the set can be empty.

    Negation and “at least” queries

    In basic RA this needs COUNT, but “at least two” is expressible with two variables forced to be different tuples:

    The ≠\neq= on the rest of the key (Essn is already equal) makes d1,d2d_1,d_2d1​,d2​ distinct. Result: John Smith, Franklin Wong. “At least kkk” needs kkk variables and (k2)\binom{k}{2}(2k​) inequalities; “exactly kkk”/counts need aggregates (not in basic calculus).

    4  Safe expressions · 8.6.8

    Theory recap
    Definition: Safe expression

    An expression is safe if it is guaranteed to produce a finite result. Precisely: the domain of an expression, dom(E)\mathrm{dom}(E)dom(E), is the set of all values that appear as constants in EEE or in any tuple of the relations referenced in EEE. EEE is safe if all values in its result are from dom(E)\mathrm{dom}(E)dom(E); otherwise it is unsafe.

    Unsafe

    { t∣not EMPLOYEE(t) }\{\,t \mid \textbf{not}\, \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t)\,\}{t∣notEMPLOYEE(t)} returns every tuple in the universe that is not an EMPLOYEE tuple: infinitely many, and their values are not in dom=\mathrm{dom} =dom= the values of EMPLOYEE. Similarly unsafe: { t∣t.Salary>50000 }\{\,t \mid t.\textsf{Salary}>50000\,\}{t∣t.Salary>50000} (no range), and { t∣R(t)orS(t)ort.A=5 }\{\,t \mid \mathrm{R}(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\mathrm{S}(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}} t.\textsf{A}=5\,\}{t∣R(t)orS(t)ort.A=5} (the third disjunct is unrestricted). The domain of Q3A is all values in EMPLOYEE, PROJECT, WORKS_ON ∪ {5}\cup\ \{5\}∪ {5}; Q3A is safe.

    How to stay safe (a sufficient, practical rule)
    • Every free variable must be restricted by a positive range atom R(t)R(t)R(t) joined by and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and to the rest of the condition (in every or\mathbin{\textbf{or}}or branch).
    • Every ∃t\exists t∃t body should contain R(t)and…R(t) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} \dotsR(t)and….
    • Every ∀t\forall t∀t body should start with not R(t)or…\textbf{not}\, R(t) \mathbin{\textbf{or}} \dotsnotR(t)or… (equivalently R(t)⇒…R(t)\Rightarrow\dotsR(t)⇒…), so only tuples of RRR are tested.
    • Use not \textbf{not}\,not only on a formula about variables that are already range-restricted (not \textbf{not}\,not is a “minus”, never a stand-alone generator).

    Following the Q3 rules gives safe expressions. Only safe expressions correspond to RA expressions.

    7  Pitfalls (how marks are lost)

    Theory recap
    1. ∀\forall∀ without the implication guard

    Writing (∀x)(PROJECT(x)andx.Dnum=4and(∃w)(… ))(\forall x)\big(\mathrm{PROJECT}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Dnum}=4\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists w)(\dots)\big)(∀x)(PROJECT(x)andx.Dnum=4and(∃w)(…)) (and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and instead of ⇒\Rightarrow⇒) demands that every tuple in the universe is a department-4 project: always FALSE, the answer is empty. Dropping only not PROJECT(x)\textbf{not}\, \mathrm{PROJECT}(x)notPROJECT(x) (keeping not (x.Dnum=4)or…\textbf{not}\, (x.\textsf{Dnum}=4)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\dotsnot(x.Dnum=4)or…) is also wrong: any non-PROJECT tuple with Dnum 4 (e.g. a hypothetical tuple outside the database) breaks it. On our evaluator both versions return nothing for department 4, while the correct Q3 returns Zelaya and Jabbar. Rule: ∀\forall∀ is always followed by not R(x)or…\textbf{not}\, R(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\dotsnotR(x)or…, or use not ∃…not \textbf{not}\, \exists\dots \textbf{not}\,not∃…not.

    2. Using ∃\exists∃ where “all” is asked

    (∃x)(PROJECT(x)andx.Dnum=4and(∃w)(… ))(\exists x)(\mathrm{PROJECT}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Dnum}=4\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists w)(\dots))(∃x)(PROJECT(x)andx.Dnum=4and(∃w)(…)) computes “works on some” department-4 project: Zelaya, Jabbar, Wong, Wallace. This is the calculus version of the RA rubric’s “the condition is existential” (0 marks for the criterion).

    3. Missing range conditions

    Every variable needs R(t)R(t)R(t): free ones with and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and, ∃\exists∃ ones inside with and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and, ∀\forall∀ ones inside with not R(t)or\textbf{not}\, R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}notR(t)or. A free variable without a range makes the expression unsafe; a ∀\forall∀ variable without one quantifies over the universe.

    4. Free variables that are not in the target list

    In { e.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(e)andDEPARTMENT(d)andd.Mgr_ssn=e.Ssn }\{\,e.\textsf{Lname} \mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(e)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(d)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}d.\textsf{Mgr\_ssn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}\,\}{e.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(e)andDEPARTMENT(d)andd.Mgr_ssn=e.Ssn} the variable ddd is free but not left of the bar: ill-formed. Write (∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)and… )(\exists d)(\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(d)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\dots)(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)and…). Conversely, a target-list variable must not be quantified.

    5. Missing join conditions / wrong scope

    nnn variables need at least n−1n-1n−1 join conditions, otherwise you get a Cartesian product (Exercise 8.27). Also keep the negated part inside the correct quantifier: not (∃x)(…not (∃w)(… ))\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\dots \textbf{not}\, (\exists w)(\dots))not(∃x)(…not(∃w)(…)), with www’s conditions referring to both eee and xxx (correlation).

    6. “At least two” without forcing distinct tuples

    (∃d1)(∃d2)(… )(\exists d_1)(\exists d_2)(\dots)(∃d1​)(∃d2​)(…) without d1.K≠d2.Kd_1.\textsf{K}\neq d_2.\textsf{K}d1​.K=d2​.K is satisfied by d1=d2d_1=d_2d1​=d2​, so it means “at least one”.

    7. NULLs

    A comparison with NULL is not TRUE: Borg has no supervisor row in Q8, and WORKS_ON(888665555, 20, NULL) fails w.Hours>10w.\textsf{Hours}>10w.Hours>10 but still counts as “works on project 20”.

    8  Domain relational calculus · 8.7

    Theory recap
    Definition: DRC expression

    Variables (domain variables) range over single values from attribute domains. A result of degree nnn needs nnn free domain variables:

    { x1,x2,…,xn∣COND(x1,…,xn,xn+1,…,xn+m) }\{\,x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n \mid \mathrm{COND}(x_1,\dots,x_n,x_{n+1},\dots,x_{n+m})\,\}{x1​,x2​,…,xn​∣COND(x1​,…,xn​,xn+1​,…,xn+m​)}

    Atoms: (1) R(x1,x2,…,xj)R(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_j)R(x1​,x2​,…,xj​) for RRR of degree jjj: TRUE iff ⟨x1,…,xj⟩\langle x_1,\dots,x_j\rangle⟨x1​,…,xj​⟩ is a tuple of RRR, by position (commas may be dropped: R(x1x2x3)R(x_1x_2x_3)R(x1​x2​x3​)); (2) xi op xjx_i\ \mathit{op}\ x_jxi​ op xj​; (3) xi op cx_i\ \mathit{op}\ cxi​ op c or c op xjc\ \mathit{op}\ x_jc op xj​. Formulas, quantifiers, free/bound and safety are as in TRC.

    Variable conventions used by the book (letters bound to attribute positions):

    EMPLOYEE(q r s t u v w x y z)(q\,r\,s\,t\,u\,v\,w\,x\,y\,z)(qrstuvwxyz)Fname, Minit, Lname, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Sex, Salary, Super_ssn, Dno
    DEPARTMENT(l m n o)(l\,m\,n\,o)(lmno)Dname, Dnumber, Mgr_ssn, Mgr_start_date
    PROJECT(h i j k)(h\,i\,j\,k)(hijk)Pname, Pnumber, Plocation, Dnum
    DEPENDENT(l m n o p)(l\,m\,n\,o\,p)(lmnop) (Q6)Essn, Dependent_name, Sex, Bdate, Relationship

    Formally every variable not left of the bar must be quantified (Q0 below quantifies 8). For brevity the book quantifies only the variables used in a condition; this is an abbreviation, not the formal notation.

    Writing calculus in the exam
    1. List the variables and their ranges first (“eee: EMPLOYEE, www: WORKS_ON, …”); for DRC list which letter is which attribute.
    2. Decide which variables are free (they give output attributes) and which are ∃\exists∃/∀\forall∀ (connectors).
    3. Write range atoms, then selection conditions, then join conditions; count joins (≥n−1\ge n-1≥n−1).
    4. For “all” write the not ∃…not ∃\textbf{not}\, \exists\dots \textbf{not}\, \existsnot∃…not∃ form, and say what happens when the set is empty.
    5. Give a one-line English reading and, if time permits, the RA equivalent and the result on the given instance.

    9  Calculus exercises

    Textbook exercises

    All COMPANY queries below were evaluated mechanically on the Figure 5.6 state (reproduced in Part I) with a small Python evaluator: tuple variables range over the whole database plus “phantom” tuples that belong to no relation (to imitate the universe), ∃\exists∃/∀\forall∀ are any/all, and every DRC formula was checked separately by binding its variables by position. TRC and DRC versions give identical results. The AIRLINE and LIBRARY queries were checked on small made-up instances (the book gives no state).

    8.10Existential and universal quantifiersE&N Ex. 8.10 · p. 281★ Must-do

    Discuss the meanings of the existential quantifier (∃\exists∃) and the universal quantifier (∀\forall∀).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Free and bound variables (needed to state the meaning)

    A tuple variable is bound if it is quantified (appears in an (∃t)(\exists t)(∃t) or (∀t)(\forall t)(∀t) clause) and free otherwise. A quantifier binds all free occurrences of its variable in the formula it governs.

    Existential quantifier (Rule 3)

    If FFF is a formula, so is (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F). It is TRUE if FFF evaluates to TRUE for some (at least one) tuple assigned to the free occurrences of ttt in FFF; otherwise FALSE. “There exists a ttt such that FFF.”

    • Used for “some”, “at least one”, and for connector variables that link the output tuple to other relations (the join is hidden inside ∃\exists∃).
    • Example (Q1): { t.Fname,t.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(t)and(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)andd.Dname=‘Research’andd.Dnumber=t.Dno) }\{\,t.\textsf{Fname},t.\textsf{Lname} \mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists d)(\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(d)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}d.\textsf{Dname}=\text{`Research'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}d.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno})\,\}{t.Fname,t.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(t)and(∃d)(DEPARTMENT(d)andd.Dname=‘Research’andd.Dnumber=t.Dno)}: employees for whom a Research department with their Dno exists (Smith, Wong, Narayan, English).
    • Over an empty range, ∃\exists∃ is FALSE.

    Universal quantifier (Rule 4)

    If FFF is a formula, so is (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F). It is TRUE if FFF evaluates to TRUE for every tuple in the universe assigned to the free occurrences of ttt in FFF; otherwise FALSE. “For all ttt, FFF.”

    • Because ttt ranges over the whole universe, the body must make every irrelevant tuple TRUE automatically: first not R(t)\textbf{not}\, R(t)notR(t) (tuples not in the relation of interest), then not C(t)\textbf{not}\, C(t)notC(t) (tuples of RRR not of interest), then the real condition. So “every ttt in RRR with CCC satisfies QQQ” is (∀t)(not R(t)ornot C(t)orQ(t))(\forall t)(\textbf{not}\, R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, C(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q(t))(∀t)(notR(t)ornotC(t)orQ(t)), i.e. (∀t)(R(t)andC(t)⇒Q(t))(\forall t)(R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} C(t)\Rightarrow Q(t))(∀t)(R(t)andC(t)⇒Q(t)).
    • Example (Q3): employees who work on every department-5 project: (∀x)(not PROJECT(x)ornot (x.Dnum=5)or(∃w)(WORKS_ON(w)andw.Essn=e.Ssnandx.Pnumber=w.Pno))(\forall x)\big(\textbf{not}\, \mathrm{PROJECT}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, (x.\textsf{Dnum}=5)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}(\exists w)(\mathrm{WORKS\_ON}(w)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}w.\textsf{Essn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Pnumber}=w.\textsf{Pno})\big)(∀x)(notPROJECT(x)ornot(x.Dnum=5)or(∃w)(WORKS_ON(w)andw.Essn=e.Ssnandx.Pnumber=w.Pno)).
    • Over an empty range (no tuple passes the guard), ∀\forall∀ is TRUE (vacuously).

    How they relate

    Each can be expressed through the other with negation (De Morgan for quantifiers):

    (∀x)(P(x))≡not (∃x)(not P(x)),(∃x)(P(x))≡not (∀x)(not P(x)),(\forall x)(P(x))\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x)),\qquad (\exists x)(P(x))\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x)),(∀x)(P(x))≡not(∃x)(notP(x)),(∃x)(P(x))≡not(∀x)(notP(x)),
    (∀x)(P(x)andQ(x))≡not (∃x)(not P(x)ornot Q(x)),(\forall x)(P(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q(x))\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, Q(x)),(∀x)(P(x)andQ(x))≡not(∃x)(notP(x)ornotQ(x)),
    (∃x)(P(x)andQ(x))≡not (∀x)(not P(x)ornot Q(x)).(\exists x)(P(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q(x))\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, Q(x)).(∃x)(P(x)andQ(x))≡not(∀x)(notP(x)ornotQ(x)).

    Moreover (∀x)(P(x))⇒(∃x)(P(x))(\forall x)(P(x))\Rightarrow (\exists x)(P(x))(∀x)(P(x))⇒(∃x)(P(x)) and not (∃x)(P(x))⇒not (∀x)(P(x))\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(P(x))\Rightarrow \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(P(x))not(∃x)(P(x))⇒not(∀x)(P(x)) (one direction only). Hence Q3 can be written without ∀\forall∀: not (∃x)(PROJECT(x)andx.Dnum=5andnot (∃w)(… ))\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\mathrm{PROJECT}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Dnum}=5\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists w)(\dots))not(∃x)(PROJECT(x)andx.Dnum=5andnot(∃w)(…)), and Q6 “no dependents” not (∃d)(DEPENDENT(d)ande.Ssn=d.Essn)\textbf{not}\, (\exists d)(\mathrm{DEPENDENT}(d)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}e.\textsf{Ssn}=d.\textsf{Essn})not(∃d)(DEPENDENT(d)ande.Ssn=d.Essn) equals (∀d)(not DEPENDENT(d)ornot (e.Ssn=d.Essn))(\forall d)(\textbf{not}\, \mathrm{DEPENDENT}(d)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, (e.\textsf{Ssn}=d.\textsf{Essn}))(∀d)(notDEPENDENT(d)ornot(e.Ssn=d.Essn)).

    Answer

    (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F) is TRUE iff at least one tuple assigned to ttt makes FFF TRUE (“some”); (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F) is TRUE iff every tuple of the universe makes FFF TRUE (“all”), so its body must be guarded as not R(t)ornot C(t)or…\textbf{not}\, R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, C(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\dotsnotR(t)ornotC(t)or…. They bind variables, are interchangeable via (∀x)P≡not (∃x)not P(\forall x)P\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)\textbf{not}\, P(∀x)P≡not(∃x)notP, and on an empty range ∃\exists∃ is FALSE while ∀\forall∀ is TRUE.

    What the grader checks

    Both meanings in terms of “some tuple” vs “every tuple of the universe”; mention of free/bound; the transformation rule; one example of each. Losing marks: describing ∀\forall∀ as “for all tuples of RRR” without saying the guard not R(t)\textbf{not}\, R(t)notR(t) is what restricts it.

    8.24Queries of Exercise 8.16 in TRC and DRCE&N Ex. 8.24 · p. 284★ Must-do

    Specify queries a, b, c, e, f, i, and j of Exercise 8.16 in both tuple and domain relational calculus.

    Exercise 8.16 (on the COMPANY schema of Figure 5.5, state of Figure 5.6): a. Retrieve the names of all employees in department 5 who work more than 10 hours per week on the ProductX project. b. List the names of all employees who have a dependent with the same first name as themselves. c. Find the names of all employees who are directly supervised by ‘Franklin Wong’. e. Retrieve the names of all employees who work on every project. f. Retrieve the names of all employees who do not work on any project. i. Find the names and addresses of all employees who work on at least one project located in Houston but whose department has no location in Houston. j. List the last names of all department managers who have no dependents.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Names” means Fname and Lname. Why: the book’s own sample queries (Q1, Q6, Q7) output these two attributes for “names”.
    2. “More than 10 hours” is strict (>10>10>10); a NULL Hours value does not satisfy it. Why: “more than” is strict, and a comparison with NULL is not TRUE.
    3. (b) “Same first name” compares DEPENDENT.Dependent_name with EMPLOYEE.Fname. Why: Dependent_name stores the dependent’s first name in Figure 5.6.
    4. (e) “Every project” means every tuple of PROJECT (all departments). If PROJECT were empty, every employee would qualify (vacuous truth). Why: the question puts no restriction on the projects.
    5. (f) A WORKS_ON tuple with Hours = NULL (Borg on project 20) still means the employee works on that project. Why: the tuple records the assignment; only the hours are unknown.
    6. (i) A department’s locations are its DEPT_LOCATIONS tuples; a project is “in Houston” if Plocation = ‘Houston’. Why: these are the only location attributes in the schema.
    7. (j) A “department manager” is an employee whose Ssn appears as some DEPARTMENT.Mgr_ssn.

    DRC variable naming (used in every part)

    EMPLOYEE(q r s t u v w x y z)(q\,r\,s\,t\,u\,v\,w\,x\,y\,z)(qrstuvwxyz)Fname, Minit, Lname, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Sex, Salary, Super_ssn, Dno
    DEPARTMENT(l m n o)(l\,m\,n\,o)(lmno)Dname, Dnumber, Mgr_ssn, Mgr_start_date
    PROJECT(h i j k)(h\,i\,j\,k)(hijk)Pname, Pnumber, Plocation, Dnum
    WORKS_ON(a b c)(a\,b\,c)(abc)Essn, Pno, Hours
    DEPENDENT(d e f g p)(d\,e\,f\,g\,p)(defgp)Essn, Dependent_name, Sex, Bdate, Relationship
    DEPT_LOCATIONS(l′ m′)(l'\,m')(l′m′)Dnumber, Dlocation

    A second copy of EMPLOYEE uses primed letters q′…z′q'\dots z'q′…z′. As in the book, only variables that occur in a condition are quantified; all other non-output variables are understood to be existentially quantified.

    (a) Department 5, more than 10 hours on ProductX

    TRC. Variables: eee EMPLOYEE (free, output), www WORKS_ON and ppp PROJECT (connectors, ∃\exists∃).

    { e.Fname,e.Lname∣ EMPLOYEE(e)ande.Dno=5and(∃w)(∃p)(WORKS_ON(w)andPROJECT(p)andp.Pname=‘ProductX’andw.Pno=p.Pnumberandw.Essn=e.Ssnandw.Hours>10) }\begin{aligned}\{\,e.\textsf{Fname},e.\textsf{Lname}\mid\ &\mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(e)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}e.\textsf{Dno}=5\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists w)(\exists p)\big(\mathrm{WORKS\_ON}(w)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{PROJECT}(p)\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}}p.\textsf{Pname}=\text{`ProductX'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}w.\textsf{Pno}=p.\textsf{Pnumber}\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}w.\textsf{Essn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}w.\textsf{Hours}>10\big)\,\}\end{aligned}{e.Fname,e.Lname∣ ​EMPLOYEE(e)ande.Dno=5and(∃w)(∃p)(WORKS_ON(w)andPROJECT(p)andp.Pname=‘ProductX’andw.Pno=p.Pnumberandw.Essn=e.Ssnandw.Hours>10)}​

    DRC.

    {q,s∣ (∃t)(∃z)(∃a)(∃b)(∃c)(∃h)(∃i)(EMPLOYEE(qrstuvwxyz)andWORKS_ON(abc)andPROJECT(hijk)andz=5anda=tandb=iandh=‘ProductX’andc>10)}\begin{aligned}\{q,s\mid\ &(\exists t)(\exists z)(\exists a)(\exists b)(\exists c)(\exists h)(\exists i)\big(\mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(qrstuvwxyz)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{WORKS\_ON}(abc)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{PROJECT}(hijk)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} z=5\mathbin{\textbf{and}} a=t\mathbin{\textbf{and}} b=i\mathbin{\textbf{and}} h=\text{`ProductX'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}} c>10\big)\}\end{aligned}{q,s∣ ​(∃t)(∃z)(∃a)(∃b)(∃c)(∃h)(∃i)(EMPLOYEE(qrstuvwxyz)andWORKS_ON(abc)andPROJECT(hijk)andz=5anda=tandb=iandh=‘ProductX’andc>10)}​

    Reading: department-5 employees for whom there is an assignment to the project named ProductX with more than 10 hours. Conditions: e.Dno=5e.\textsf{Dno}=5e.Dno=5, p.Pname=‘ProductX’p.\textsf{Pname}=\text{`ProductX'}p.Pname=‘ProductX’, w.Hours>10w.\textsf{Hours}>10w.Hours>10 are selections; w.Pno=p.Pnumberw.\textsf{Pno}=p.\textsf{Pnumber}w.Pno=p.Pnumber, w.Essn=e.Ssnw.\textsf{Essn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}w.Essn=e.Ssn are the two joins (3 variables, 2 joins). RA:

    T1←σDno=5(EMPLOYEE)⋈Ssn=EssnσHours>10(WORKS_ON)RESULT←πFname, Lname(T1⋈Pno=PnumberσPname=‘ProductX’(PROJECT))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{T1} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Dno=5}}\left(EMPLOYEE\right)\mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Ssn=Essn}}}\sigma_{\text{Hours$>$10}}\left(WORKS\_ON\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Fname, Lname}}\left(\mathit{T1}\mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Pno=Pnumber}}}\sigma_{\text{Pname=`ProductX'}}\left(PROJECT\right)\right)\end{array}T1RESULT​←←​σDno=5​(EMPLOYEE)⋈Ssn=Essn​σHours>10​(WORKS_ON)πFname, Lname​(T1⋈Pno=Pnumber​σPname=‘ProductX’​(PROJECT))​

    Result: John Smith (32.5 h), Joyce English (20 h).

    (b) Dependent with the same first name

    TRC: { e.Fname,e.Lname∣ EMPLOYEE(e)and(∃d)(DEPENDENT(d)andd.Essn=e.Ssnandd.Dependent_name=e.Fname) }\begin{aligned}\text{TRC: }\{\,e.\textsf{Fname},e.\textsf{Lname}\mid\ &\mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(e)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists d)\big(\mathrm{DEPENDENT}(d)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}d.\textsf{Essn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}d.\textsf{Dependent\_name}=e.\textsf{Fname}\big)\,\}\end{aligned}TRC: {e.Fname,e.Lname∣ ​EMPLOYEE(e)and(∃d)(DEPENDENT(d)andd.Essn=e.Ssnandd.Dependent_name=e.Fname)}​

    Answer

    Results on Figure 5.6: (a) John Smith, Joyce English; (b) none; (c) John Smith, Ramesh Narayan, Joyce English; (e) none; (f) none; (i) Jennifer Wallace, 291 Berry, Bellaire, TX; (j) Borg. Formulas as above (TRC and DRC give identical results).

    What the grader checks (adapted from the RA rubrics)
    • Assumptions with reasons (“names”, strict >>>, how NULL Hours and empty sets are handled): typically 1 mark per query.
    • Every join present: nnn variables, ≥n−1\ge n-1≥n−1 join atoms. A missing w.Essn=e.Ssnw.\textsf{Essn}=e.\textsf{Ssn}w.Essn=e.Ssn is a Cartesian product: 0 for that criterion.
    • (e) is universal: an answer equivalent to “works on some project” gets 0 for the “all” criterion; a ∀\forall∀ without not PROJECT(p)\textbf{not}\, \mathrm{PROJECT}(p)notPROJECT(p) loses it too.
    • Correlation: in (i) the not ∃\textbf{not}\, \existsnot∃ must be tied to eee’s Dno; in (e) the inner ∃w\exists w∃w must mention both eee and ppp.
    • Free variables only in the target list; every other variable quantified. Exact output attributes (Address in (i), only Lname in (j)).
    • DRC: one variable per attribute position, in schema order; equal letters or an explicit === for joins.
    8.25AIRLINE queries in TRC and DRCE&N Ex. 8.25 · p. 284

    Specify queries a, b, c, and d of Exercise 8.17 in both tuple and domain relational calculus.

    Exercise 8.17 (AIRLINE schema, Figure 5.8): a. For each flight, list the flight number, the departure airport for the first leg of the flight, and the arrival airport for the last leg of the flight. b. List the flight numbers and weekdays of all flights or flight legs that depart from Houston Intercontinental Airport (airport code ‘iah’) and arrive in Los Angeles International Airport (airport code ‘lax’). c. List the flight number, departure airport code, scheduled departure time, arrival airport code, scheduled arrival time, and weekdays of all flights or flight legs that depart from some airport in the city of Houston and arrive at some airport in the city of Los Angeles. d. List all fare information for flight number ‘co197’.

    Relevant relations of Figure 5.8: AIRPORT(Airport_code, Name, City, State); FLIGHT(Flight_number, Airline, Weekdays); FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time); FARE(Flight_number, Fare_code, Amount, Restrictions). (Also LEG_INSTANCE, AIRPLANE_TYPE, CAN_LAND, AIRPLANE, SEAT_RESERVATION, not needed here.)

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Legs of a flight are numbered in travel order, so the first leg has the smallest Leg_number of that flight and the last leg the largest. Why: the schema has no other ordering attribute; using “smallest” rather than “Leg_number = 1” does not depend on the numbering starting at 1.
    2. (b), (c) “Flights or flight legs that depart from X and arrive in Y” is read at the leg level: some leg of the flight goes from X to Y. Why: airport codes are stored only in FLIGHT_LEG; a one-leg flight is covered too. (The alternative reading, “the flight’s first leg departs X and its last leg arrives Y”, is given at the end of (b).)
    3. Airport codes are stored in lower case as in the question (‘iah’, ‘lax’); the city names are ‘Houston’ and ‘Los Angeles’. Weekdays come from FLIGHT.

    DRC variables: FLIGHT(f a w)(f\,a\,w)(faw); FLIGHT_LEG(f l d t r s)(f\,l\,d\,t\,r\,s)(fldtrs) = (Flight_number, Leg_number, Dep. code, Sched. dep. time, Arr. code, Sched. arr. time), subscripts for further copies; AIRPORT(c n y e)(c\,n\,y\,e)(cnye) = (code, Name, City, State); FARE(f c a r)(f\,c\,a\,r)(fcar). Repeating the same variable in two atoms is an equality (join) condition.

    (a) First-leg departure and last-leg arrival of each flight

    TRC. l1l_1l1​ is the first leg (no leg of the same flight with a smaller number), l2l_2l2​ the last leg (none larger).

    { l1.Flight_number, l1.Departure_airport_code, l2.Arrival_airport_code∣FLIGHT_LEG(l1)andFLIGHT_LEG(l2)andl1.Flight_number=l2.Flight_numberandnot (∃x)(FLIGHT_LEG(x)andx.Flight_number=l1.Flight_numberandx.Leg_number<l1.Leg_number)andnot (∃y)(FLIGHT_LEG(y)andy.Flight_number=l2.Flight_numberandy.Leg_number>l2.Leg_number) }\begin{aligned}\{\,&l_1.\textsf{Flight\_number},\ l_1.\textsf{Departure\_airport\_code},\ l_2.\textsf{Arrival\_airport\_code}\mid\\ &\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(l_1)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(l_2)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l_1.\textsf{Flight\_number}=l_2.\textsf{Flight\_number}\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)\big(\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Flight\_number}=l_1.\textsf{Flight\_number}\\&\qquad \mathbin{\textbf{and}}x.\textsf{Leg\_number}<l_1.\textsf{Leg\_number}\big)\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists y)\big(\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(y)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}y.\textsf{Flight\_number}=l_2.\textsf{Flight\_number}\\&\qquad \mathbin{\textbf{and}}y.\textsf{Leg\_number}>l_2.\textsf{Leg\_number}\big)\,\}\end{aligned}{​l1​.Flight_number, l1​.Departure_airport_code, l2​.Arrival_airport_code∣FLIGHT_LEG(l1​)andFLIGHT_LEG(l2​)andl1​.Flight_number=l2​.Flight_numberandnot(∃x)(FLIGHT_LEG(x)andx.Flight_number=l1​.Flight_numberandx.Leg_number<l1​.Leg_number)andnot(∃y)(FLIGHT_LEG(y)andy.Flight_number=l2​.Flight_numberandy.Leg_number>l2​.Leg_number)}​

    DRC.

    {f,d1,r2∣ (∃l1)(∃l2)(FLIGHT_LEG(f l1 d1 t1 r1 s1)andFLIGHT_LEG(f l2 d2 t2 r2 s2)andnot (∃l3)(FLIGHT_LEG(f l3 d3 t3 r3 s3)andl3<l1)andnot (∃l4)(FLIGHT_LEG(f l4 d4 t4 r4 s4)andl4>l2))}\begin{aligned}\{f,d_1,r_2\mid\ &(\exists l_1)(\exists l_2)\big(\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(f\,l_1\,d_1\,t_1\,r_1\,s_1)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(f\,l_2\,d_2\,t_2\,r_2\,s_2)\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists l_3)(\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(f\,l_3\,d_3\,t_3\,r_3\,s_3)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} l_3<l_1)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists l_4)(\mathrm{FLIGHT\_LEG}(f\,l_4\,d_4\,t_4\,r_4\,s_4)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} l_4>l_2)\big)\}\end{aligned}{f,d1​,r2​∣ ​(∃l1​)(∃l2​)(FLIGHT_LEG(fl1​d1​t1​r1​s1​)andFLIGHT_LEG(fl2​d2​t2​r2​s2​)andnot(∃l3​)(FLIGHT_LEG(fl3​d3​t3​r3​s3​)andl3​<l1​)andnot(∃l4​)(FLIGHT_LEG(fl4​d4​t4​r4​s4​)andl4​>l2​))}​

    Reading: pair the leg with no predecessor with the leg with no successor of the same flight. This is the “min/max without aggregates” pattern (a negated ∃\exists∃ with <<< / >>>). A one-leg flight gives l1=l2l_1=l_2l1​=l2​ (correct: first and last leg coincide).

    (b) Legs from ‘iah’ to ‘lax’

    8.26LIBRARY queries in TRC and DRCE&N Ex. 8.26 · p. 285

    Specify queries c, d, and f of Exercise 8.18 in both tuple and domain relational calculus.

    Exercise 8.18 (LIBRARY schema, Figure 8.14): c. Retrieve the names of all borrowers who do not have any books checked out. d. For each book that is loaned out from the Sharpstown branch and whose Due_date is today, retrieve the book title, the borrower’s name, and the borrower’s address. f. Retrieve the names, addresses, and number of books checked out for all borrowers who have more than five books checked out.

    Figure 8.14: BOOK(Book_id, Title, Publisher_name); BOOK_AUTHORS(Book_id, Author_name); PUBLISHER(Name, Address, Phone); BOOK_COPIES(Book_id, Branch_id, No_of_copies); BOOK_LOANS(Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no, Date_out, Due_date); LIBRARY_BRANCH(Branch_id, Branch_name, Address); BORROWER(Card_no, Name, Address, Phone).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. A book is “checked out” by a borrower iff there is a BOOK_LOANS tuple with that Card_no. Why: returned loans are not kept (there is no return date), so BOOK_LOANS holds the current loans.
    2. “Today” is a date constant TODAY\mathit{TODAY}TODAY substituted when the query is run. Why: calculus has no built-in current-date function.
    3. (f) “Number of books checked out” counts BOOK_LOANS tuples (key Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no), so two tuples are different loans iff they differ in Book_id or Branch_id. Why: that is the key of BOOK_LOANS for a fixed borrower.

    DRC variables: BOOK(k t p)(k\,t\,p)(ktp); BOOK_LOANS(k b c o u)(k\,b\,c\,o\,u)(kbcou) = (Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no, Date_out, Due_date); LIBRARY_BRANCH(b m z)(b\,m\,z)(bmz); BORROWER(c n a h)(c\,n\,a\,h)(cnah).

    (c) Borrowers with no books checked out

    TRC: { b.Name∣BORROWER(b)andnot (∃l)(BOOK_LOANS(l)andl.Card_no=b.Card_no) }\text{TRC: }\{\,b.\textsf{Name} \mid \mathrm{BORROWER}(b)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists l)\big(\mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(l)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l.\textsf{Card\_no}=b.\textsf{Card\_no}\big)\,\}TRC: {b.Name∣BORROWER(b)andnot(∃l)(BOOK_LOANS(l)andl.Card_no=b.Card_no)}
    DRC: {n∣(∃c)(BORROWER(c n a h)andnot (∃c2)(BOOK_LOANS(k b c2 o u)andc2=c))}\text{DRC: }\{n\mid (\exists c)\big(\mathrm{BORROWER}(c\,n\,a\,h)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, (\exists c_2)(\mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(k\,b\,c_2\,o\,u)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} c_2=c)\big)\}DRC: {n∣(∃c)(BORROWER(cnah)andnot(∃c2​)(BOOK_LOANS(kbc2​ou)andc2​=c))}

    Reading: no loan carries the borrower’s card number. RA:

    πName((πCard_no(BORROWER)−πCard_no(BOOK_LOANS))∗BORROWER)\pi_{\text{Name}}\left((\pi_{\text{Card\_no}}\left(BORROWER\right)-\pi_{\text{Card\_no}}\left(BOOK\_LOANS\right))\mathbin{*} BORROWER\right)πName​((πCard_no​(BORROWER)−πCard_no​(BOOK_LOANS))∗BORROWER)

    (d) Sharpstown loans due today: title, borrower’s name and address

    { k.Title,b.Name,b.Address∣BOOK(k)andBORROWER(b)and(∃l)(∃r)(BOOK_LOANS(l)andLIBRARY_BRANCH(r)andr.Branch_name=‘Sharpstown’andl.Branch_id=r.Branch_idandl.Due_date=TODAYandl.Book_id=k.Book_idandl.Card_no=b.Card_no) }\begin{aligned}\{\,&k.\textsf{Title},b.\textsf{Name},b.\textsf{Address}\mid\\&\mathrm{BOOK}(k)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{BORROWER}(b)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists l)(\exists r)\big(\mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(l)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}(r)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}r.\textsf{Branch\_name}=\text{`Sharpstown'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l.\textsf{Branch\_id}=r.\textsf{Branch\_id}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l.\textsf{Due\_date}=\mathit{TODAY}\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l.\textsf{Book\_id}=k.\textsf{Book\_id}\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l.\textsf{Card\_no}=b.\textsf{Card\_no}\big)\,\}\end{aligned}{​k.Title,b.Name,b.Address∣BOOK(k)andBORROWER(b)and(∃l)(∃r)(BOOK_LOANS(l)andLIBRARY_BRANCH(r)andr.Branch_name=‘Sharpstown’andl.Branch_id=r.Branch_idandl.Due_date=TODAYandl.Book_id=k.Book_idandl.Card_no=b.Card_no)}​
    DRC: {t,n,a∣ (∃k)(∃b)(∃c)(∃u)(∃m)(BOOK(k t p)andBOOK_LOANS(k b c o u)andLIBRARY_BRANCH(b m z)andBORROWER(c n a h)andm=‘Sharpstown’andu=TODAY)}\begin{aligned}\text{DRC: }\{t,n,a\mid\ &(\exists k)(\exists b)(\exists c)(\exists u)(\exists m)\big(\mathrm{BOOK}(k\,t\,p)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(k\,b\,c\,o\,u)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}(b\,m\,z)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{BORROWER}(c\,n\,a\,h)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}} m=\text{`Sharpstown'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}} u=\mathit{TODAY}\big)\}\end{aligned}DRC: {t,n,a∣ ​(∃k)(∃b)(∃c)(∃u)(∃m)(BOOK(ktp)andBOOK_LOANS(kbcou)andLIBRARY_BRANCH(bmz)andBORROWER(cnah)andm=‘Sharpstown’andu=TODAY)}​

    Four variables (TRC), three join conditions (lll–rrr, lll–kkk, lll–bbb): the loan is the hub. In DRC the joins are the shared letters kkk, bbb, ccc.

    (f) More than five books checked out

    The number of books is an aggregate (COUNT): it cannot be output in basic TRC/DRC, which have no aggregate functions (the book’s Exercise 8.31 asks for such an extension). The selection “more than five” = “at least six” can be expressed with six loan variables that are pairwise different:

    { b.Name,b.Address∣ BORROWER(b)and(∃l1)⋯(∃l6)(⋀i=16(BOOK_LOANS(li)andli.Card_no=b.Card_no)and⋀1≤i<j≤6(li.Book_id≠lj.Book_idorli.Branch_id≠lj.Branch_id)) }\begin{aligned}\{\,b.\textsf{Name},b.\textsf{Address}\mid\ &\mathrm{BORROWER}(b)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists l_1)\cdots (\exists l_6)\Big(\\&\textstyle\bigwedge_{i=1}^{6}\big(\mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(l_i)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l_i.\textsf{Card\_no}=b.\textsf{Card\_no}\big)\\ &\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textstyle\bigwedge_{1\le i<j\le 6}\big(l_i.\textsf{Book\_id}\neq l_j.\textsf{Book\_id}\\&\qquad \mathbin{\textbf{or}}l_i.\textsf{Branch\_id}\neq l_j.\textsf{Branch\_id}\big)\Big)\,\}\end{aligned}{b.Name,b.Address∣ ​BORROWER(b)and(∃l1​)⋯(∃l6​)(⋀i=16​(BOOK_LOANS(li​)andli​.Card_no=b.Card_no)and⋀1≤i<j≤6​(li​.Book_id=lj​.Book_idorli​.Branch_id=lj​.Branch_id))}​
    DRC: {n,a∣ (∃c)(BORROWER(c n a h)and(∃k1)(∃b1)⋯(∃k6)(∃b6)(⋀i=16BOOK_LOANS(ki bi c oi ui)and⋀1≤i<j≤6(ki≠kjorbi≠bj)))}\begin{aligned}\text{DRC: }\{n,a\mid\ &(\exists c)\Big(\mathrm{BORROWER}(c\,n\,a\,h)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}(\exists k_1)(\exists b_1)\cdots (\exists k_6)(\exists b_6)\big(\\&\qquad\textstyle\bigwedge_{i=1}^{6}\mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(k_i\,b_i\,c\,o_i\,u_i)\\&\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textstyle\bigwedge_{1\le i<j\le6}(k_i\neq k_j\mathbin{\textbf{or}} b_i\neq b_j)\big)\Big)\}\end{aligned}DRC: {n,a∣ ​(∃c)(BORROWER(cnah)and(∃k1​)(∃b1​)⋯(∃k6​)(∃b6​)(⋀i=16​BOOK_LOANS(ki​bi​coi​ui​)and⋀1≤i<j≤6​(ki​=kj​orbi​=bj​)))}​

    (the big and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and stands for its 666 and (62)=15\binom{6}{2}=15(26​)=15 conjuncts written out). To also report the number, the calculus must be extended with aggregates, e.g. a term COUNT{l∣BOOK_LOANS(l)andl.Card_no=b.Card_no}\mathrm{COUNT}\{l\mid \mathrm{BOOK\_LOANS}(l)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}l.\textsf{Card\_no}=b.\textsf{Card\_no}\}COUNT{l∣BOOK_LOANS(l)andl.Card_no=b.Card_no} in the target list (this is what SQL’s GROUP BY Card_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 does).

    Answer

    (c), (d) as above. (f): names and addresses of borrowers with ≥6\ge 6≥6 distinct loans are expressible with six pairwise-distinct variables; the count column itself is not expressible in basic relational calculus (needs an aggregate extension). Checked on a test instance: (c) returns the borrower with no loans, (d) the one Sharpstown loan due today, (f) only the borrower with exactly six loans (not the one with five).

    What the grader checks

    (f) is where marks are lost: claiming a COUNT in pure calculus without saying it is an extension, or “at least six” with variables not forced distinct (then one loan satisfies all six variables). State the limitation.

    8.27Minimum number of join conditionsE&N Ex. 8.27 · p. 285

    In a tuple relational calculus query with nnn tuple variables, what would be the typical minimum number of join conditions? Why? What is the effect of having a smaller number of join conditions?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Minimum number: n−1n-1n−1

    Think of a graph whose nodes are the nnn tuple variables and whose edges are join conditions (like the query graph of Section 8.6.5). For every variable to be related to the others the graph must be connected, and a connected graph on nnn nodes needs at least n−1n-1n−1 edges (a spanning tree). So the typical minimum is n−1n-1n−1 join conditions (a join on a composite key, e.g. WORKS_ON’s (Essn, Pno), may need several atoms for one “edge”).

    Check against the book

    Q1: ttt, ddd (2 variables) and 1 join (d.Dnumber=t.Dnod.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno}d.Dnumber=t.Dno). Q2: ppp, mmm, ddd and 2 joins (p.Dnum=d.Dnumberp.\textsf{Dnum}=d.\textsf{Dnumber}p.Dnum=d.Dnumber, d.Mgr_ssn=m.Ssnd.\textsf{Mgr\_ssn}=m.\textsf{Ssn}d.Mgr_ssn=m.Ssn). Q3′'′: eee, xxx, www and 2 joins.

    Effect of fewer join conditions

    With fewer than n−1n-1n−1 joins the graph splits into disconnected groups, and the condition places no restriction between them: the result contains every combination of tuples of the separate groups, i.e. a Cartesian product. Consequences: (i) the result is semantically wrong (spurious combinations, e.g. every employee paired with every Research department if d.Dnumber=t.Dnod.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno}d.Dnumber=t.Dno is dropped from Q1, which then returns all 8 employees); (ii) the result is much larger and costly to compute. (If an unjoined variable is ∃\exists∃-quantified, its condition degenerates to “some such tuple exists anywhere”, which is again not what was meant.)

    Answer

    Typically n−1n-1n−1 join conditions, because the nnn variables must be linked into one connected structure (a spanning tree of the query graph). Fewer joins leave some variables unrelated, producing Cartesian-product combinations: wrong (spurious) results and a much larger result.

    8.28DRC queries in the abbreviated notationE&N Ex. 8.28 · p. 285

    Rewrite the domain relational calculus queries that followed Q0 in Section 8.7 in the style of the abbreviated notation of Q0A, where the objective is to minimize the number of domain variables by writing constants in place of variables wherever possible.

    Q0A: {u,v∣EMPLOYEE(‘John’,‘B’,‘Smith’,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)}\{u,v\mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(\text{`John'},\text{`B'},\text{`Smith'},t,u,v,w,x,y,z)\}{u,v∣EMPLOYEE(‘John’,‘B’,‘Smith’,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)}. The queries after Q0 are Q1, Q2, Q6, Q7 (reproduced in Part I, Section 7).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. In the abbreviated notation, every variable not left of the bar is implicitly existentially quantified (as stated for Q0A), and using the same variable in two atoms expresses an equality (join) condition. Why: this is QBE’s convention, on which Q0A is based; it removes both the constant-selection atoms and the join atoms.
    2. For negation (Q6), variables that occur only inside the negated atom are existentially quantified inside the not \textbf{not}\,not. Why: “no dependent with Essn ttt” means not ∃\textbf{not}\, \existsnot∃, not ∃not \exists \textbf{not}\,∃not.

    Two techniques: a constant replaces a variable and its selection atom (l=‘Research’l=\text{`Research'}l=‘Research’); a shared variable replaces a variable and its join atom (m=zm=zm=z).

    Q1: {q,s,v∣EMPLOYEE(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)andDEPARTMENT(‘Research’,z,n,o)}Q2: {i,k,s,u,v∣PROJECT(h,i,‘Stafford’,k)andDEPARTMENT(l,k,n,o)andEMPLOYEE(q,r,s,n,u,v,w,x,y,z)}Q6: {q,s∣EMPLOYEE(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)andnot DEPENDENT(t,m,n,o,p)}Q6A: same as Q6 (the ∀ form collapses to the same abbreviated query)Q7: {s,q∣EMPLOYEE(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)andDEPARTMENT(h,i,t,k)andDEPENDENT(t,m,n,o,p)}\begin{aligned} Q1:&\ \{q,s,v\mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(\text{`Research'},z,n,o)\}\\ Q2:&\ \{i,k,s,u,v\mid \mathrm{PROJECT}(h,i,\text{`Stafford'},k)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(l,k,n,o)\\&\qquad \mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(q,r,s,n,u,v,w,x,y,z)\}\\ Q6:&\ \{q,s\mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, \mathrm{DEPENDENT}(t,m,n,o,p)\}\\ Q6A:&\ \text{same as Q6 (the }\forall\text{ form collapses to the same abbreviated query)}\\ Q7:&\ \{s,q\mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{DEPARTMENT}(h,i,t,k)\\&\qquad \mathbin{\textbf{and}}\mathrm{DEPENDENT}(t,m,n,o,p)\} \end{aligned}Q1:Q2:Q6:Q6A:Q7:​ {q,s,v∣EMPLOYEE(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)andDEPARTMENT(‘Research’,z,n,o)} {i,k,s,u,v∣PROJECT(h,i,‘Stafford’,k)andDEPARTMENT(l,k,n,o)andEMPLOYEE(q,r,s,n,u,v,w,x,y,z)} {q,s∣EMPLOYEE(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)andnotDEPENDENT(t,m,n,o,p)} same as Q6 (the ∀ form collapses to the same abbreviated query) {s,q∣EMPLOYEE(q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z)andDEPARTMENT(h,i,t,k)andDEPENDENT(t,m,n,o,p)}​

    8.29“At least those projects” via the rules for ∀\forall∀ and IF–THENE&N Ex. 8.29 · p. 285★ Must-do

    Consider this query: Retrieve the Ssns of employees who work on at least those projects on which the employee with Ssn=123456789 works. This may be stated as (FORALL xxx) (IF PPP THEN QQQ), where

    • xxx is a tuple variable that ranges over the PROJECT relation.
    • P≡P\equivP≡ employee with Ssn=123456789 works on project xxx.
    • Q≡Q\equivQ≡ employee eee works on project xxx.

    Express the query in tuple relational calculus, using the rules

    • (∀x)(P(x))≡not (∃x)(not (P(x)))(\forall x)(P(x))\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, (P(x)))(∀x)(P(x))≡not(∃x)(not(P(x))).

    10  Exam cheat sheet

    Calculus at a glance

    • Declarative: calculus says what, RA says how (procedural). TRC: variables range over tuples (basis of SQL); DRC: over values (basis of QBE).
    • Same power: basic RA ≡\equiv≡ safe TRC ≡\equiv≡ safe DRC. Relationally complete = can express every basic-RA query. SQL is complete and adds aggregates, grouping, ordering (none in basic calculus).

    TRC syntax and meaning

    • Form: { t1.Aj,…,tn.Am∣COND(t1,…,tn+m) }\{\,t_1.A_j,\dots,t_n.A_m \mid \mathrm{COND}(t_1,\dots,t_{n+m})\,\}{t1​.Aj​,…,tn​.Am​∣COND(t1​,…,tn+m​)}. Needs (1) a range R(t)R(t)R(t) per variable, (2) selection + join conditions, (3) target list left of the bar.
    • Example: { t.Fname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000 }\{\,t.\textsf{Fname} \mid \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\textsf{Salary}>50000\,\}{t.Fname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000}.
    • Atoms (3): R(t)R(t)R(t) (range atom); t.A op s.Bt.A\ \mathit{op}\ s.Bt.A op s.B (join); t.A op ct.A\ \mathit{op}\ ct.A op c (selection), op∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,≠}\mathit{op}\in\{=,<,\le,>,\ge,\neq\}op∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,=}.
    • Formulas: atoms; F1andF2F_1\mathbin{\textbf{and}} F_2F1​andF2​, F1orF2F_1\mathbin{\textbf{or}} F_2F1​orF2​, not F\textbf{not}\, FnotF; (∃t)F(\exists t)F(∃t)F (TRUE for some tuple); (∀t)F(\forall t)F(∀t)F (TRUE for every tuple in the universe).
    • Free/bound: occurrence in an atom is free; and/or/not \mathbin{\textbf{and}}/\mathbin{\textbf{or}}/\textbf{not}\,and/or/not keep status; ∃t\exists t∃t/∀t\forall t∀t bind the free ttt’s. E.g. in (∃t)(d.Dnumber=t.Dno)(\exists t)(d.\textsf{Dnumber}=t.\textsf{Dno})(∃t)(d.Dnumber=t.Dno): ddd free, ttt bound.
    • Golden rule: free variables = exactly those left of the bar; all others ∃\exists∃/∀\forall∀-bound. Free ≈\approx≈ outer FROM; ∃\exists∃ ≈\approx≈ correlated EXISTS.

    Quantifier transformation rules

    • (∀x)P≡not (∃x)(not P)(\forall x)P \equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P)(∀x)P≡not(∃x)(notP);  (∃x)P≡not (∀x)(not P)(\exists x)P \equiv \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P)(∃x)P≡not(∀x)(notP).
    • (∀x)(PandQ)≡not (∃x)(not Pornot Q)(\forall x)(P\mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, Q)(∀x)(PandQ)≡not(∃x)(notPornotQ); (∀x)(PorQ)≡not (∃x)(not Pandnot Q)(\forall x)(P\mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, Q)(∀x)(PorQ)≡not(∃x)(notPandnotQ).
    • (∃x)(PorQ)≡not (∀x)(not Pandnot Q)(\exists x)(P\mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, Q)(∃x)(PorQ)≡not(∀x)(notPandnotQ); (∃x)(PandQ)≡not (∀x)(not Pornot Q)(\exists x)(P\mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, Q)(∃x)(PandQ)≡not(∀x)(notPornotQ).
    • Implication: P⇒Q≡not PorQP\Rightarrow Q \equiv \textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{or}} QP⇒Q≡notPorQ;  not (P⇒Q)≡Pandnot Q\textbf{not}\, (P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, Qnot(P⇒Q)≡PandnotQ.
    • One way only: (∀x)P⇒(∃x)P(\forall x)P\Rightarrow (\exists x)P(∀x)P⇒(∃x)P;  not (∃x)P⇒not (∀x)P\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)P\Rightarrow \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)Pnot(∃x)P⇒not(∀x)P.
    • Informal rule: swap quantifier + put not \textbf{not}\,not in front; and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and↔\leftrightarrow↔or\mathbin{\textbf{or}}or; negated ↔\leftrightarrow↔ un-negated.
    • Empty range: ∃\exists∃ is FALSE, ∀\forall∀ is TRUE (vacuous).
    • Derivation to write in the exam:
      (∀x)(not R(x)ornot C(x)orQ(x))(\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, R(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, C(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}} Q(x))(∀x)(notR(x)ornotC(x)orQ(x))
      ≡not (∃x)(R(x)andC(x)andnot Q(x))\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(R(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} C(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, Q(x))≡not(∃x)(R(x)andC(x)andnotQ(x)) (“no xxx in RRR with CCC fails QQQ”).

    Safe expressions

    • Safe = guaranteed finite result: every result value is in dom(E)\mathrm{dom}(E)dom(E) (constants of EEE + values in referenced relations). Only safe expressions map to RA.
    • Unsafe: { t∣not EMPLOYEE(t) }\{\,t \mid \textbf{not}\, \mathrm{EMPLOYEE}(t)\,\}{t∣notEMPLOYEE(t)}; { t∣t.Salary>50000 }\{\,t \mid t.\textsf{Salary}>50000\,\}{t∣t.Salary>50000} (no range); { t∣R(t)ort.A=5 }\{\,t \mid R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}} t.A=5\,\}{t∣R(t)ort.A=5}.
    • Stay safe: free var: R(t)and…R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\dotsR(t)and… in every or\mathbin{\textbf{or}}or branch; ∃t\exists t∃t: R(t)and…R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\dotsR(t)and…; ∀t\forall t∀t: not R(t)or…\textbf{not}\, R(t)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\dotsnotR(t)or…; not \textbf{not}\,not only on already-ranged variables (a minus, never a generator).

    Traps that cost marks

    • ∀\forall∀ with and\mathbin{\textbf{and}}and instead of the guard:
      (∀x)(PROJECT(x)and… )(\forall x)(\mathrm{PROJECT}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\dots)(∀x)(PROJECT(x)and…) needs every universe tuple to be a project: always empty. Dropping only not R(x)\textbf{not}\, R(x)notR(x) is also wrong.
    • ∃\exists∃ where “all” is asked: gives “works on some”: 0 for the “all” criterion.
    • Direction reversed: not (∃x)(not PandQ)\textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q)not(∃x)(notPandQ) instead of (Pandnot Q)(P\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textbf{not}\, Q)(PandnotQ) computes “only”.
    • Missing range R(t)R(t)R(t): unsafe (free) or quantifies over the universe (∀\forall∀).
    • Free var not in target list (or a target var quantified): ill-formed; wrap it in (∃d)(… )(\exists d)(\dots)(∃d)(…).
    • Joins: nnn variables need ≥n−1\ge n-1≥n−1 join atoms, else Cartesian product. Inner ∃w\exists w∃w must mention both eee and xxx (correlation).
    • Same variable reused for two different WORKS_ON rows forces them equal: use www and vvv.
    • At least kkk without ≠\neq= means at least one. COUNT is not in pure calculus: say it is an extension.
    • NULLs: a comparison with NULL is not TRUE (Borg in Q8; NULL Hours fails >10>10>10).
    • DRC: a dropped attribute must be ∃\exists∃-quantified; letters in schema order.

    Exam moves

    • List variables and ranges first (“eee: EMPLOYEE, www: WORKS_ON”); for DRC, which letter is which attribute.
    • Decide free (output) vs ∃/∀\exists/\forall∃/∀ (connectors); write ranges, then selections, then joins; count joins.
    • For “all” write the not ∃…not ∃\textbf{not}\, \exists\dots \textbf{not}\, \existsnot∃…not∃ form, show ∀=not ∃not \forall=\textbf{not}\, \exists \textbf{not}\,∀=not∃not + De Morgan, and state the empty-set (vacuous) case.
    • State assumptions with reasons (strict >>>, NULL handling, empty sets).
    • Finish with a one-line English reading, the RA equivalent and the result on the instance.
